originalGroup.material:
A. A label can be another kind of doorway

At the entrance to a small history museum, visitors could choose a large-print guide. It contained all the information printed beside the objects, but in bigger letters. The guide seemed an obvious way to make the exhibition easier to use. Then a visitor asked a question that the museum's designer, Ellis, had not expected: 'How do I know which page goes with the object in front of me?'

Ellis followed several visitors through the rooms. The labels used collection numbers, while the guide arranged objects by date. To match one with the other, visitors had to find a small number, remember it and search through the guide. Larger letters did not remove those steps. For someone who found small text difficult to read, the first step could be the hardest of all.

The museum could not immediately replace every label. Instead, Ellis added a large, simple symbol beside each group of objects and repeated it at the top of the relevant guide pages. He chose symbols with different outlines rather than relying only on colours. The guide's information stayed in date order, but its symbols offered another route into it.

During a trial, visitors reached the right pages more quickly. One person, however, found a symbol confusing because it looked like a direction arrow. Ellis changed that design before making the guides available throughout the museum. The staff also kept a few copies of the earlier version so that they could explain exactly what had changed.

The project did not solve every access problem. Some visitors still needed audio descriptions or help moving between rooms. For Ellis, its lesson was that making information physically readable was only part of the task. People also needed a clear connection between the information and the thing they were trying to understand.

B. Listening to the quiet part of a delivery

When a food distributor replaced several diesel delivery vehicles with electric ones, residents near its city depot welcomed the quieter engines. The company expected fewer complaints about early-morning deliveries. Yet in the following month, calls about noise hardly changed. The manager, Pavel, decided to spend a morning on a delivery route rather than order another survey.

From inside the vehicle, the route seemed much quieter. Outside it, Pavel noticed sounds that had previously been hidden by the engine. Metal wheels struck cracks in the pavement. Empty containers knocked together as they were loaded. At one shop, a driver had to pull a heavy cage over a raised doorway because the unloading space was blocked by boxes.

Pavel first considered moving deliveries to later in the morning. Shop owners explained that this would leave staff unloading goods while serving customers. He therefore asked drivers and shop workers to identify places where a small change could make a difference. They cleared the blocked doorway, replaced damaged wheels and tested soft covers that kept empty containers from hitting one another.

The team did not put soft wheels on every cage at once. A pair that worked well on smooth floors was harder to push over rough outdoor surfaces. Drivers compared several designs on actual routes before the company chose replacements. They also agreed on a simple rule: when possible, lift the final empty container into the vehicle rather than throw it onto the others.

Complaints declined over the next two months. Pavel was careful not to credit the change to a single piece of equipment. The quieter vehicles had helped him hear the rest of the problem, but the improvement came from treating the delivery as a whole sequence of actions. Technology had opened an opportunity; attention to ordinary movements had made more of it.

questions.prompt: Why did Pavel join a delivery route?
questions.material:
B. Listening to the quiet part of a delivery

When a food distributor replaced several diesel delivery vehicles with electric ones, residents near its city depot welcomed the quieter engines. The company expected fewer complaints about early-morning deliveries. Yet in the following month, calls about noise hardly changed. The manager, Pavel, decided to spend a morning on a delivery route rather than order another survey.

From inside the vehicle, the route seemed much quieter. Outside it, Pavel noticed sounds that had previously been hidden by the engine. Metal wheels struck cracks in the pavement. Empty containers knocked together as they were loaded. At one shop, a driver had to pull a heavy cage over a raised doorway because the unloading space was blocked by boxes.

Pavel first considered moving deliveries to later in the morning. Shop owners explained that this would leave staff unloading goods while serving customers. He therefore asked drivers and shop workers to identify places where a small change could make a difference. They cleared the blocked doorway, replaced damaged wheels and tested soft covers that kept empty containers from hitting one another.

The team did not put soft wheels on every cage at once. A pair that worked well on smooth floors was harder to push over rough outdoor surfaces. Drivers compared several designs on actual routes before the company chose replacements. They also agreed on a simple rule: when possible, lift the final empty container into the vehicle rather than throw it onto the others.

Complaints declined over the next two months. Pavel was careful not to credit the change to a single piece of equipment. The quieter vehicles had helped him hear the rest of the problem, but the improvement came from treating the delivery as a whole sequence of actions. Technology had opened an opportunity; attention to ordinary movements had made more of it.

options.text: The distributor had stopped receiving customer orders.
The electric vehicles could no longer reach the city centre.
Noise complaints had stayed high despite quieter engines.
Residents wanted the company to return to diesel vehicles.

questions.explanation: 第一段电动车上线后噪声投诉几乎未变，所以经理随车观察。未说无订单、车辆无法进城或居民要求恢复柴油。

originalGroup.material:
A. More than a shorter line on the map

A riverside path had been closed for years because two short sections were difficult to maintain after heavy rain. When the town announced plans to reopen it, the first design connected the sections with a straight paved track. On a map, the new line looked simple and efficient. People who lived nearby were pleased that the route might finally return.

Before the plan was approved, landscape designer Anika invited residents to walk along the accessible parts with her. She asked them to point out places where they usually stopped. An older man showed her a low wall sheltered from the wind. A parent described a wide corner where children could wait safely while adults caught up. Several people mentioned a bend where the river became audible even when it was hidden by trees.

None of these places appeared as a destination on the design map. The straight track would pass behind the sheltered wall and cut off the wide corner. It would also take walkers farther from the bend. Anika realised that the path's usefulness had never depended only on the time needed to travel from one end to the other.

The final route still used a firm surface through the wet sections, but it curved towards the wall and kept the waiting space. At the bend, the team made a small opening in the existing barrier so that visitors using wheelchairs could reach the stopping point without entering soft ground. They did not remove the trees simply to give everyone the same view.

A year after reopening, the town counted more users, although it had no reliable count from before the closure for a direct comparison. Anika considered the conversations recorded during planning equally important. They had revealed what a clean line on a map could miss: a route can be valuable partly because it gives people reasons to pause.

B. A calendar with space for the unexpected

At the beginning of the term, Erin created a study calendar in which every evening was carefully divided. Maths filled one hour, history another, and reading the final half hour before bed. She was pleased with its neat appearance. By the second week, however, she was already working on tasks that the calendar said should have been finished days before.

Erin initially blamed herself for failing to follow the plan. Then her tutor asked her to keep a record of what actually happened for five days. The record contained more than time spent studying. It showed a bus arriving late, a younger brother needing help with a project, and a science assignment that required finding a missing library book. None of these appeared in the original calendar.

The tutor did not suggest abandoning plans. Instead, she asked Erin to estimate tasks from recent experience, identify which deadlines could not move and leave some time unassigned. Erin also separated starting a task from finishing it. An essay could begin with choosing evidence on Monday, even if a complete draft would not be ready until Wednesday.

In the revised calendar, three evenings included a short spare block. If nothing unexpected happened, Erin could use it to review notes or stop work a little earlier. When a club meeting ran late, she moved unfinished reading into one of those blocks instead of taking time from sleep. She checked the plan at the end of each week and adjusted the following one.

The new version looked less impressive on the wall because it contained more empty space. It also worked better. Erin came to see planning as a way to make decisions before feeling rushed, rather than a promise that the week would contain no surprises. The empty blocks were not signs of missing effort; they were part of the work the plan was doing.

questions.prompt: What did Erin's five-day record help her recognise?
questions.material:
B. A calendar with space for the unexpected

At the beginning of the term, Erin created a study calendar in which every evening was carefully divided. Maths filled one hour, history another, and reading the final half hour before bed. She was pleased with its neat appearance. By the second week, however, she was already working on tasks that the calendar said should have been finished days before.

Erin initially blamed herself for failing to follow the plan. Then her tutor asked her to keep a record of what actually happened for five days. The record contained more than time spent studying. It showed a bus arriving late, a younger brother needing help with a project, and a science assignment that required finding a missing library book. None of these appeared in the original calendar.

The tutor did not suggest abandoning plans. Instead, she asked Erin to estimate tasks from recent experience, identify which deadlines could not move and leave some time unassigned. Erin also separated starting a task from finishing it. An essay could begin with choosing evidence on Monday, even if a complete draft would not be ready until Wednesday.

In the revised calendar, three evenings included a short spare block. If nothing unexpected happened, Erin could use it to review notes or stop work a little earlier. When a club meeting ran late, she moved unfinished reading into one of those blocks instead of taking time from sleep. She checked the plan at the end of each week and adjusted the following one.

The new version looked less impressive on the wall because it contained more empty space. It also worked better. Erin came to see planning as a way to make decisions before feeling rushed, rather than a promise that the week would contain no surprises. The empty blocks were not signs of missing effort; they were part of the work the plan was doing.

options.text: Most school tasks could be completed without any preparation.
Her original plan had left no space for ordinary interruptions.
Her bus was late on every journey throughout the term.
Her tutor wanted her to stop planning her studies.
